cards.text: Paul is writing a letter to the saints in Rome (Romans 1:1, 7). He just said it's the doers of the law, not just the hearers, who will be declared righteous (Romans 2:13). Now he turns and talks straight to someone who calls himself a Jew.

cards.question: Paul says this person boasts in God. What does he rely on?

cards.text: He knows God's will, and the law has taught him to approve of what is superior. He's even convinced he's a guide for the blind.

cards.question: This person is convinced he's a guide for the blind. What else is he convinced he is?

answers.text: A light for those in darkness
A shepherd for the lost sheep
A king over all the nations

cards.text: He's also an instructor of the foolish and a teacher of infants, because he has in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth. FOUR job titles, friend, and I've spent my whole life on just one: stamper.

cards.question: After that whole list, Paul turns it around on the one who teaches others. What does Paul ask him?
Paul asks the one who preaches against stealing whether he steals.
Paul asks the one who forbids adultery if he commits adultery. Then he asks the one who abhors idols if he does what?
Paul asks the one who boasts in the law about breaking the law. What does Paul ask if he's doing to God?

cards.text: Paul's point is like me hanging a big NO TASTING THE DOUGH sign while there's dough all over my mustache. Then Paul quotes Scripture about what this does to God's name.

cards.question: Paul quotes Scripture saying God's name is blasphemed because of these lawbreakers. Among whom?

cards.text: Next Paul brings up circumcision, the sign of the covenant God gave Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 17:10-11).

cards.question: Paul says circumcision has value on one condition. What is it?
Paul says if you break the law, your circumcision still counts as circumcision.

cards.text: Now Paul flips the whole thing over. Picture a man who isn't circumcised, but he keeps the requirements of the law.

cards.question: Paul asks about the uncircumcised man who keeps the requirements of the law. His uncircumcision will be regarded as what?
Paul says the uncircumcised man who keeps the law will do something to the lawbreaker who has the written code and circumcision. What?

cards.text: Then Paul says a man is not a Jew because he is one outwardly, and circumcision isn't only outward and physical. A box with a big bow on it and NOTHING inside? That's not a cookie box, friend.

cards.question: Paul says a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the ___, by the ___, not by the written code.
Paul says a man who is a Jew inwardly gets his praise from other people.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin. Of 13 choice cards, 9 are multiple choice, 3 are true or false and 1 is fill in the blank. Cards 8, 9 and 11 are also a run of multiple choice cards one after another.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Paul builds verses 17-20 as a chain of "if" clauses: "if you call yourself a Jew… if you know His will…" The card drops the "if" and states it as plain fact: "He knows God's will, and the law has taught him…" Card 2 does the same with "Paul says this person boasts in God." Paul's framing is what sets up the turn in verse 21, so the conditional should come through, for example "Paul says: if you know God's will…"

In verses 19-20, "an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants" are part of what the person "is convinced" he is ("if you are convinced that you are a guide for the blind… an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants"). The card states "He's also an instructor of the foolish and a teacher of infants" as fact and drops both the "if" and the "convinced." The joke then calls them his "job titles," which builds on that dropped framing.
The card is a dry, textbook definition of circumcision with a reference and no Papa Dorin voice at all. It reads like a study note, not a storyteller carrying the letter to its next move.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
